base-convert.title: Base Conversion Tool
base-convert.intro: A base conversion tool that instantly converts between binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal, with real-time results and automatic detection of 0b/0o/0x prefixes
base-convert.toolIntroTitle: Base Conversion: Understanding How Computers Think with 0s and 1s
base-convert.problemTitle: 1. Why Programmers Must Master Base Conversion
base-convert.problem1: At the hardware level, computers only have two states — powered on or off, high voltage or low voltage, 1 or 0. All text, images, and videos are ultimately encoded as long strings of binary digits. But binary is extremely unfriendly to humans — the ordinary integer 255 is 11111111 in binary, requiring eight bits to represent just a two-digit decimal number. So we invented octal, decimal, and hexadecimal as "human-friendly" intermediate representations — base conversion is the translation between these representations.
base-convert.problem2: This tool supports real-time conversion between binary, octal, decimal, and hexadecimal. Enter a number in any base, and the other three bases update synchronously and instantly. It supports decimal fractions, negative numbers, and automatic base detection — no need to manually select "which base is this." The tool auto-detects based on number characteristics (e.g., 0x prefix for hexadecimal, 0b prefix for binary).
base-convert.problem3: Beyond numerical conversion, it also provides "bit width visualization" — displaying numbers as 8-bit/16-bit/32-bit binary with each bit annotated with its weight value (128, 64, 32...1). For students learning computer architecture, embedded engineers debugging low-level protocols, or security researchers analyzing network packets, this is the most intuitive base learning tool.
base-convert.formatTitle: 2. Technical Background of the Four Number Systems
base-convert.formatBin: Binary (Base-2): The computer's "native language." Each binary digit (bit) can only store 0 or 1; 8 bits form a byte, representing 0–255 (256 values). Memory addresses, CPU registers, network protocol data frames — everything at the lowest level is binary. Reading binary directly is extremely difficult for humans, which is why we need other bases as "bridges."
base-convert.formatOct: Octal (Base-8): Widely used in early computer systems — because 8 = 2³, every 3 binary bits map exactly to 1 octal digit, making conversion extremely convenient. In modern programming languages, octal literals start with 0 (e.g., 0755 for file permissions rwxr-xr-x). The Linux chmod command still uses octal today.
base-convert.formatDec: Decimal (Base-10): The most commonly used base by humans — because we have ten fingers. But in computers, decimal-to-binary conversion can produce infinite repeating fractions (e.g., 0.1 in binary is 0.0001100110011... repeating infinitely) — which is why floating-point arithmetic has precision issues (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3).
base-convert.formatHex: Hexadecimal (Base-16): The most commonly used base in modern programming — because 16 = 2⁴, every 4 binary bits map exactly to 1 hex digit. Color values (#FF0000 = red), memory addresses (0x7FFF5FBFF8C0), Unicode code points (U+4E2D = 中) — all use hexadecimal. It's 4× more compact than binary and easier to convert to/from binary than decimal.
base-convert.featuresTitle: 3. Core Features of the Conversion Tool
base-convert.featureRealTime: Real-time Conversion: Enter a number in any base input field, and the other three bases update instantly — no need to click a "Convert" button. Implemented based on JavaScript's parseInt/toString methods, with BigInt support for very large numbers.
base-convert.featureCopy: One-click Copy: Each base result has a copy button — convenient for pasting into code, documents, or terminals.
base-convert.featurePreset: Common Value Presets: Built-in quick-load for common values like 255 (0xFF), 1024 (0x400), 65535 (0xFFFF) — one click to see how these "programmer numbers" are represented in all four bases.
base-convert.featureAutoDetect: Auto Base Detection: Numbers starting with 0x are auto-detected as hexadecimal, 0b as binary, 0 as octal — no manual base switching needed.
base-convert.usageSelectBase: Select the source base: Click the base tabs above (BIN/OCT/DEC/HEX) to choose the base of the number you enter.
base-convert.usageInputNumber: Enter a number: Type the number to convert into the input box, and it will be converted in real time automatically.
base-convert.usageViewResult: View results: The result is shown simultaneously in four formats: binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal.
base-convert.usageCopyResult: Copy results: Click the "Copy" button next to each result to copy that base's value individually, or click "Copy All" to copy all results at once.
base-convert.usagePreset: Use presets: Click a preset tag below (e.g., 255, 1024, 0xFF) to quickly fill in common values for conversion.
base-convert.formatDetailBin: Binary Display: Shows the number as 8/16/32-bit binary with each bit annotated with its weight value. Intuitively understand "why 255 = 11111111" — every bit is 1, and the sum of weights = 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255.
base-convert.formatDetailOct: Octal Display: Groups binary every 3 bits, corresponding to one octal digit. E.g., 11111111 → 0377.
base-convert.formatDetailDec: Decimal Display: Shows the decimal representation of the number — the format most familiar to humans.
base-convert.formatDetailHex: Hexadecimal Display: Groups binary every 4 bits, corresponding to one hex digit. E.g., 11111111 → 0xFF.
base-convert.shortcutEnter: Press Enter to trigger the conversion.
base-convert.shortcutSwitch: When you switch bases, the current input value is automatically converted to the new base's representation.
base-convert.formatRule2: Octal: Only accepts 0-7. E.g., 755, 644. Note that Linux file permissions use octal notation.
base-convert.range1: The supported value range is -2^53 ~ 2^53 (JavaScript's safe integer range).
base-convert.range2: Very large numbers beyond the safe range may lose precision.
base-convert.range3: For negative numbers, the hexadecimal result is displayed as a minus sign followed by the hexadecimal representation of the absolute value.
base-convert.security1: Pure Front-end Computation: All base conversions are performed in the browser — no data is uploaded.
base-convert.security2: No Network Dependency: Works normally offline after the page has loaded.
base-convert.faqConvertError: Q: Conversion error? A: Check if the input contains illegal characters — e.g., a 2 in binary, or an 8 in octal.
base-convert.faqValueAbnormal: Q: Imprecise decimal fraction conversion? A: Some decimal fractions are infinite repeating decimals in other bases (e.g., 0.1 repeats infinitely in binary). The tool truncates to a reasonable precision.
base-convert.faqCopyFailed: Q: Copy not working? A: Some browsers require user authorization for clipboard access. If copy fails, you can manually select the result text to copy.
base-convert.msgInvalidNumber: Cannot parse as a valid number

regex.title: Regex Tester
regex.desc: An online regex testing tool for testing and validating regular expressions, with real-time matching and replacement, and support for multiple regex flavors
regex.flagsHint: Flags: g Global  i Case-insensitive  m Multiline  s Dot matches newline  u Unicode
regex.presetsTitle: Common Regex Cheat Sheet (Click to Fill)
regex.introTitle: Regular Expressions: The Swiss Army Knife for Text Processing
regex.problemsTitle: 1. Why Regular Expressions Are Both Loved and Hated
regex.problem1: Test and validate regular expressions with real-time matching and replacement.
regex.problem2: This tool provides a visual regex testing environment — enter a regex pattern and test text, and the tool instantly highlights all matches, showing match positions, capture group content, and match statistics. Supports both JavaScript and Python regex syntax.
regex.problem3: Use it online anytime, anywhere, without installing professional software.
regex.formatRegex: General Syntax: Regular expressions consist of literal characters and metacharacters. ^ matches the start, $ matches the end, . matches any character, * matches 0 or more, + matches 1 or more, ? matches 0 or 1, [] matches character sets, () groups and captures, | means alternation.
regex.formatJs: JavaScript Syntax: Supports /pattern/flags literal syntax. Common flags: g (global match), i (case-insensitive), m (multiline mode). Supports named capture groups (?...) and lookaheads/lookbehinds (?=...) / (?!...).
regex.formatPython: Python Style Reference: Although the browser uses the JavaScript regex engine, this tool's syntax cheat sheet also annotates equivalent syntax for Python's re module. Most basic syntax (character classes, quantifiers, groups) is shared between both styles; some advanced features (like named group syntax) differ.
regex.featureOnline: Real-time Matching: After entering a regex pattern, matches are instantly highlighted in the test text — no need to click a "Test" button. Modifying the regex or test text updates results in real time.
regex.featurePreview: Real-time Preview: Results are displayed instantly for easy adjustment and confirmation.
regex.featureExport: One-click Export: Quickly export processed files or copy results.
regex.featureSecurity: Data Security: All data is processed locally and never uploaded to any server.
regex.guideInputRegex: Enter a regex pattern: Type the pattern you want to test in the regex input box, e.g. \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}.
regex.guideSelectFlags: Select flags: Click the flag buttons to set regex flags (g: global match, i: case-insensitive, m: multiline mode, s: dot matches newline, u: Unicode).
regex.guideInputText: Enter test text: Enter the text to match in the test text area.
regex.guideRealtime: Real-time matching: The system displays matching results in real time and highlights all matches.
regex.guideDetails: View match details: See detailed information for each match in the list below, including position, length, and capture groups.
regex.guideLocate: Locate a match: Click the "Locate" button to jump to the highlighted position of the corresponding match.
regex.guideSwitchReplace: Switch to Replace: Click the "Replace" tab to switch to replacement mode.
regex.guideSetRegex: Enter a regex pattern: Set the pattern to match.
regex.guideInputSource: Enter original text: Enter the content to replace in the original text area.
regex.guideSetReplace: Set replacement content: Enter the replacement content in the "Replace With" input box, supporting capture group references like $1, $2.
regex.guideDoReplace: Run the replacement: Click the "Replace" button or wait for the automatic replacement.
regex.guideClickPreset: Click a preset: Click a preset regex below to fill it in quickly.
regex.guidePresetContent: Preset content: Includes common regexes for dates, phone numbers, emails, URLs, IP addresses, ID card numbers, Chinese characters, blank lines, HTML tags, hex colors, numbers, words, and more.
regex.syntaxCharClass: Character classes: . matches any character, \d matches a digit, \w matches a letter, digit, or underscore, \s matches whitespace.
regex.syntaxQuantifier: Quantifiers: * zero or more, + one or more, ? zero or one, {n} exactly n, {n,m} between n and m.
regex.syntaxAnchor: Anchors: ^ start of line, $ end of line, \b word boundary.
regex.syntaxCharSet: Character sets: [abc] matches a, b, or c; [^abc] matches any character except a, b, and c.
regex.notesEscape: Special characters must be escaped, such as \, ., *, +, ?, (), [], {}, ^, $, |.
regex.notesDoubleEscape: In JavaScript regexes, backslashes need double escaping, e.g. \\d.
regex.notesGroupNumbering: Capture groups are numbered starting from $1; $0 represents the full match.
regex.flagGlobal: g (Global): Find all matches instead of only the first one.
regex.flagInsensitive: i (Case-insensitive): Match without distinguishing uppercase and lowercase.
regex.flagMultiline: m (Multiline): ^ and $ match the start and end of every line.
regex.flagDotAll: s (Dot matches newline): . can match line break characters.
regex.perfComplex: Complex regex patterns may cause performance issues, especially when processing large amounts of text.
regex.perfGreedy: Avoid greedy quantifiers (*, +); consider using lazy quantifiers (*?, +?).
regex.perfLargeText: Testing very large text (over 100KB) may cause the browser to lag.
regex.securityLocal: All processing is done locally in your browser; data is never uploaded to any server.
regex.securityPublicDevice: It is recommended not to process text containing sensitive information on public devices.
regex.faqSyntax: Syntax error: Check whether special characters in the regex pattern are escaped correctly.
regex.faqNoMatch: No matches: Verify the pattern and test text are correct, and check the flag settings.
regex.faqPartialMatch: Incomplete matches: Make sure the g (global) flag is enabled.
regex.faqReplaceIssue: Replacement issues: Check whether the capture group references in the replacement content are correct.
regex.msgInputRequired: Please enter a regex pattern and text

sql.title: SQL Formatter
sql.intro: An online SQL formatter that beautifies SQL statements for better readability and maintainability, with syntax highlighting, standard and compact output layouts, and customizable options such as indentation, keyword case, and blank lines between statements
sql.inputPlaceholder: Enter or paste your SQL statement...
sql.outputPlaceholder: The formatted SQL will be displayed here...
sql.infoIntro: SQL Formatting: Making Database Queries Clearly Readable
sql.problem1: Format SQL statements to improve readability and maintainability.
sql.problem2: This tool supports two modes: formatting and compression. Formatting arranges SQL statements in a standard style — uppercase keywords, clause line breaks, indented conditions. Compression removes all extra whitespace, producing compact single-line SQL.
sql.problem3: Use it online anytime, anywhere, without installing professional software.
sql.formatSql: Standard SQL: ANSI SQL standard syntax — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, etc. The common foundation shared by all databases.
sql.formatMysql: MySQL: Supports MySQL-specific syntax — backtick quoting (`table_name`), LIMIT pagination, GROUP_CONCAT, IFNULL, etc.
sql.formatPostgresql: PostgreSQL: Supports PG-specific syntax — double-quote quoting ("table_name"), RETURNING clauses, LATERAL JOIN, JSON operators (->>), etc.
sql.featureOnline: Smart Formatting: Auto-recognizes SQL keywords and clause structure — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY each get their own line, with conditional expressions indented by level.
sql.featurePreview: Real-time Preview: Results are displayed instantly for easy adjustment and confirmation.
sql.featureExport: One-click Export: Quickly export the processed file or copy the result.
sql.featureSecurity: Data Security: All data is processed locally and never uploaded to any server.
sql.usageFormat: Format: Converts compressed or messy SQL code into a well-structured, properly indented format for easier reading and maintenance.
sql.usageCompress: Compress: Compresses formatted SQL into a compact form, removing extra whitespace to reduce file size.
sql.usageCopy: Copy Result: Copy the formatted or compressed code to the clipboard with one click.
sql.usageSample: Sample SQL: Click the "Sample SQL" button to load sample SQL and automatically format it with the current options.
sql.usageClear: Clear: Quickly clear all input and output content.
sql.optFormatStyle: Output Format: In Standard format, each clause keyword occupies its own line with fields indented below; in Compact format, clause content stays on the same line as its keyword while JOIN clauses remain on indented lines (default: Standard).
sql.optIndent: Indent: Choose 2 spaces, 4 spaces, or Tab as the indentation unit (default: 4 spaces).
sql.optUppercase: Keywords: Choose uppercase, lowercase, or preserve original case (default: preserve original).
sql.optLinesBetween: Blank Lines Between Statements: Set the number of blank lines between SQL statements (default: 1).
sql.syntaxManip: Data Manipulation: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, VALUES, SET
sql.syntaxDefine: Data Definition: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TABLE, INDEX, VIEW, DATABASE
sql.syntaxClause: Query Clauses: ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, LIMIT, OFFSET
sql.syntaxCondition: Conditional Expressions: AND, OR, NOT, IN, LIKE, BETWEEN, IS NULL
sql.syntaxControl: Flow Control: CASE, WHEN, THEN, ELSE, END
sql.syntaxAggregate: Aggregate Functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
sql.shortcut1: Both the input and output areas support independent copy operations.
sql.shortcut2: The status bar displays the line count, character count, and keyword count in real time.
sql.noteSemicolon: SQL statements must end with a semicolon ;.
sql.noteQuotes: Strings must be wrapped in single or double quotes.
sql.noteBacktick: Identifiers (table names, column names) can be wrapped in backticks `.
sql.noteUpper: When "Uppercase" is selected, all SQL keywords are converted to uppercase.
sql.noteLower: When "Lowercase" is selected, all SQL keywords are converted to lowercase.
sql.notePreserve: When "Preserve Original" is selected, keywords keep their original case.
sql.noteFunctions: Function names are converted to uppercase by default.
sql.noteLarge: Processing very large SQL files (over 1MB) may cause the browser to lag.
sql.noteSegment: It is recommended to process large SQL files in segments.
sql.noteLocal: All processing is done in your local browser; data is never uploaded to any server.
sql.noteSensitive: Avoid processing SQL code containing sensitive information on shared or public devices.
sql.faqFormatFail: Formatting Failed: Check whether the SQL syntax is correct, especially that parentheses and quotes are matched.
sql.faqKeywordNotConverted: Keywords Not Converted: Make sure the correct keyword case option is selected.
sql.faqCopyFail: Copy Failed: Check whether the browser allows clipboard access.

cron.title: Cron Expression Parser
cron.intro: A Cron expression parser supporting both 5-field and 6-field formats, providing expression parsing, generation, and next-execution-time prediction
cron.specialCharLegend: * Any value  , List  - Range  / Step  ? No specific value  L Last  W Nearest weekday  # Nth weekday of month
cron.infoIntro: Cron Expression Parsing: Making Scheduled Tasks No Longer a Guessing Game
cron.problemsTitle: 1. Cron Expressions Are the 'Secret Language' of Ops Engineers
cron.problem1: 0 0/30 9-17 ? * MON-FRI — this seemingly cryptic string means "execute every 30 minutes during workdays from 9 AM to 5 PM." Cron expressions are the universal syntax for scheduled tasks in Linux systems and Java/Node.js applications — 5 or 6 fields, each using special symbols to represent time rules. A typo won't throw an error, but the task might execute at 3 AM and drive you crazy.
cron.problem2: This tool supports parsing, generating, and validating Cron expressions. Enter any Cron expression and the tool parses each field's meaning, displays a human-readable description, and predicts the next 10 execution times. You can also work backwards — select minute/hour/day/month/weekday through a visual interface, and the tool auto-generates the corresponding Cron expression.
cron.problem3: Supports both 5-field (standard Linux Cron) and 6-field (extended Cron with seconds, e.g., Spring/Quartz) formats. Built-in common presets — every minute, every hour, daily at midnight, every 30 minutes on workdays, etc. — one click to load, no need to memorize the syntax.
cron.formatStandard5: Standard 5-field Format (Linux crontab): Minute Hour Day Month Weekday. No seconds field; minimum precision is 1 minute. Suitable for Linux/Unix crontab scheduled tasks, GitHub Actions workflow scheduling, Docker container auto-restart, etc.
cron.formatExtended6: Extended 6-field Format (Spring/Quartz): Second Minute Hour Day Month Weekday. Includes a seconds field; minimum precision is 1 second. Suitable for Spring Task, Quartz Scheduler, XXL-Job, and other Java task scheduling frameworks. Supports additional special characters (L, W, #, etc.).
cron.formatSpecialChars: Special Characters Reference: * matches all values (every), , lists multiple values, - specifies a range, / specifies a step interval, L means last (6-field format), W means nearest weekday (6-field format), # means Nth weekday of month (6-field format).
cron.featureParse: Real-time Expression Parsing: Instantly parses each field's meaning after entering a Cron expression, describing the execution rules in natural language (e.g., "Every day at 9:30 AM", "1st and 15th of each month at 2 AM"). Parsing results update in real time as you modify the expression, helping you understand the actual execution logic of complex expressions.
cron.featureGenerate: Visual Expression Generation: No need to memorize syntax — select values for each time field via dropdown menus, and the system auto-generates the corresponding Cron expression. Supports exact values, ranges, steps, enumerations, and more. Generated expressions can be directly copied into crontab or scheduler framework configurations.
cron.featurePredict: Execution Time Prediction: Based on Cron expression parsing rules, accurately calculates the next 10 execution time points. Predictions account for leap years, days per month, weekday cycles, and other calendar rules. If predicted times don't match expectations, the expression is likely wrong — this is the most effective way to verify expression correctness.
cron.featureFormatSwitch: 5-field/6-field Format Switching: One-click switching between standard 5-field and extended 6-field formats. The system auto-adjusts the field structure (adding or removing the seconds field) while keeping other field values unchanged. Convenient for migrating scheduled task configurations between Linux crontab and Java scheduling frameworks.
cron.usageInput: Enter Expression: Paste or type a Cron expression (5-field or 6-field format) in the input box. The system auto-detects the format and parses each field's meaning. Results are displayed in natural language below — e.g., 0 30 9 * * 1-5 is parsed as "Every Monday to Friday at 9:30 AM."
cron.usageAutoParse: Auto-parse Update: Modify any character in the expression, and the parsing result updates instantly. No button click needed. You can adjust the expression character by character and watch the natural language description change in real time, helping you understand the role of each syntax element.
cron.usageVisual: Visual Timeline: Below the parsing result, a visual timeline shows the next 10 execution time points. Each time point is annotated with the specific date and time for intuitive verification of whether the expression meets expectations. If the interval or distribution of time points seems unreasonable, the expression needs adjustment.
cron.usageExecTime: Execution Time Details: Each predicted execution time point can be clicked for detailed information — including full date/time, day of week, and time interval from now. This information helps you assess whether the task execution frequency is reasonable.
cron.usagePresets: Common Preset Templates: Provides commonly used Cron expression presets — every minute (* * * * *), every hour (0 * * * *), daily at 2 AM (0 2 * * *), every Monday at 9 AM (0 9 * * 1), 1st of each month at midnight (0 0 1 * *), etc. Click a preset tag to quickly fill it in.
cron.usageGenMode: Select Generation Mode: Generate expressions by selecting time values field by field via dropdown menus. Each field supports three selection modes — "Every" (*), "Specific Value" (e.g., 9 o'clock), "Range" (e.g., 9-17), "Step" (e.g., every 5 minutes), "Enumeration" (e.g., 1,3,5).
cron.usageGenFormat: Select Format Standard: Choose between 5-field format (Linux crontab) and 6-field format (Spring/Quartz). The 6-field format adds a seconds field for second-level precision scheduling.
cron.usageGenSecond: Seconds Field (6-field format): Select the seconds matching rule — every second (*), specific second (e.g., 0), range (e.g., 0-30), step (e.g., every 10 seconds), or enumerate multiple second values.
cron.usageGenMinute: Minutes Field: Select the minutes matching rule — every minute (*), specific minute (e.g., 30), range (e.g., 0-30), step (e.g., every 15 minutes), or enumerate multiple minute values.
cron.usageGenHour: Hours Field: Select the hours matching rule — every hour (*), specific hour (e.g., 9), range (e.g., 9-17 for work hours), step (e.g., every 2 hours), or enumerate multiple hour values.
cron.usageGenDay: Day Field: Select the date matching rule — every day (*), specific date (e.g., 1st), range (e.g., 1-15), step (e.g., every 5 days), or enumerate multiple dates. The 6-field format also supports L (last day) and W (nearest weekday).
cron.usageGenMonth: Month Field: Select the month matching rule — every month (*), specific month (e.g., January), range (e.g., March-November), step (e.g., quarterly), or enumerate multiple months. Supports both numbers (1-12) and English abbreviations (JAN-DEC).
cron.usageGenWeekday: Weekday Field: Select the weekday matching rule — every day (*), specific weekday (e.g., Monday), range (e.g., Monday-Friday), enumerate multiple weekdays. Supports numbers (0-7, where both 0 and 7 represent Sunday) and English abbreviations (MON-SUN). The 6-field format also supports # syntax (e.g., 1#3 means the third Monday).
cron.usageGenResult: View Generated Result: Selected field values are automatically combined into a complete Cron expression, displayed at the top of the editor. Below the expression, execution rules are described in natural language, and the next 10 execution time predictions are shown. Once confirmed correct, you can copy it with one click.
cron.usageFmt5: 5-field Syntax: Minute Hour Day Month Weekday. Field ranges: minute 0-59, hour 0-23, day 1-31, month 1-12, weekday 0-7 (0 and 7 are both Sunday). Supports * , - / special characters.
cron.usageFmt6: 6-field Syntax: Second Minute Hour Day Month Weekday. Adds a seconds field (0-59) to the 5-field format. Additionally supports L (last), W (nearest weekday), # (Nth weekday) special characters.
cron.usageFmtSecond: Seconds Field (6-field only): Range 0-59. Supports * , - / special characters. E.g., 0/30 means every 30 seconds.
cron.usageFmtMinute: Minutes Field: Range 0-59. E.g., */15 means every 15 minutes, 0,30 means at minute 0 and 30 of every hour.
cron.usageFmtHour: Hours Field: Range 0-23. E.g., 9-17 means 9 AM to 5 PM, */2 means every 2 hours.
cron.usageFmtDay: Day Field: Range 1-31 (note: not all months have 31 days). E.g., 1,15 means the 1st and 15th of each month, L means the last day of the month (6-field format only).
cron.usageFmtMonth: Month Field: Range 1-12 or JAN-DEC. E.g., 1,4,7,10 means the first month of each quarter, */3 means every 3 months.
cron.usageFmtWeekday: Weekday Field: Range 0-7 or SUN-SAT (0 and 7 both represent Sunday). E.g., 1-5 means Monday to Friday, 1#3 means the third Monday of each month (6-field format only).
cron.scAsterisk: *: Any value — matches all possible values for that field (every).
cron.scDash: -: Range — specifies a continuous range, e.g., 1-5.
cron.scSlash: /: Step — specifies an interval, e.g., */5 means every 5 units.
cron.scQuestion: ?: No specific value — typically used when day and weekday fields conflict.
cron.scL: L: Last — e.g., L in the day field means the last day of the month.
cron.noteFormat1: 5-field and 6-field formats cannot be mixed. Linux crontab only supports 5-field format (no seconds); using 6-field format in crontab will cause parsing errors. Spring/Quartz uses 6-field format and requires a seconds field.
cron.noteFormat2: When both day and weekday fields are specified (non-*), the task executes when either condition is met (OR relationship). For example, 0 0 15 * 5 means "execute at midnight on the 15th of each month OR every Friday" — not "the 15th that is also a Friday." For AND logic, you need the 6-field format's special syntax.
cron.noteFormat3: In the weekday field, both 0 and 7 represent Sunday — this is a legacy compatibility design. It's recommended to use 0 for Sunday to avoid confusion. Some systems also support English abbreviations (MON, TUE, etc.), but not all implementations support them.
cron.noteExample1: * * * * * — Execute every minute. Suitable for high-frequency monitoring tasks like health checks and heartbeat detection.
cron.noteExample2: 0 2 * * * — Execute daily at 2 AM. Suitable for daily maintenance tasks like database backups, log rotation, and cache clearing.
cron.noteExample3: 0 9 * * 1-5 — Execute at 9 AM every weekday. Suitable for workday tasks like timed report generation and data synchronization.
cron.noteExample4: 0 0 1 * * — Execute at midnight on the 1st of each month. Suitable for monthly tasks like report generation, billing settlement, and quota resets.
cron.noteExample5: */5 * * * * — Execute every 5 minutes. Suitable for near-real-time tasks like metrics collection, queue checking, and email sending.
cron.noteExample6: 0 0 * * 0 — Execute at midnight every Sunday. Suitable for weekly tasks like data aggregation, index optimization, and temp file cleanup.
cron.noteExample7: 0 30 9,18 * * * — Execute at 9:30 AM and 6:30 PM daily (6-field format). Suitable for twice-daily tasks like notifications and data sync.
cron.notePredict1: Execution time prediction is based on standard Cron expression parsing rules, accounting for all Gregorian calendar rules — including leap years (Feb 29), long/short months (30/31 days), weekday cycles, etc. Predictions are consistent with actual execution times of Linux crontab and mainstream scheduling frameworks.
cron.notePredict2: If predicted times include unreasonable dates (e.g., Feb 30), the expression may have logical errors. Check whether the day and month field ranges are compatible.
cron.notePredict3: Timezone matters: Cron expressions themselves don't contain timezone information; execution time depends on the server's system timezone. Predictions use the browser's local timezone, which may differ from the server's actual execution time.
cron.noteSecurity1: Cron expression parsing and prediction calculations are entirely completed locally in the browser via the JavaScript engine. Entered expressions are never uploaded to any server. Even in offline environments (after the page has loaded), all features work normally.
cron.noteSecurity2: Cron expressions themselves don't contain sensitive data — they're just descriptions of time rules. But if your scheduled tasks involve sensitive operations (like database backups), avoid editing task configurations on screens in public places to prevent bystanders from seeing scheduling information.
cron.faqParseFail:
Expression parsing failed?
Check if the expression format is correct — whether the field count is 5 or 6, and whether each field's value is within the valid range. Common errors include: using commas instead of spaces between fields, using special characters not supported by the current format, or field values out of range (e.g., writing 60 for minutes).
cron.faqExecTime:
Predicted execution times are wrong?
Confirm the selected format standard (5-field/6-field) matches the target system. Check if the browser timezone matches the server timezone. If both day and weekday fields have non-* values, they have an OR relationship, not AND.
cron.faqCopyFail:
Copy not working?
Check if the browser allows clipboard access for this site. You can also manually select the expression text and use Ctrl+C to copy.
cron.faqNoChange:
Prediction didn't change after modifying the expression?
Confirm the modified characters actually affected the expression's meaning. For example, changing */5 to */10 changes the frequency, but just adjusting whitespace (like extra leading spaces) won't change the parsing result.

cron.formatTitle: 2. The Six Fields of Cron Expressions
cron.formatCode128: Seconds (optional): 0-59, supports * (every second), / (interval), - (range), , (list). The first field in 6-field Cron. 5-field standard Cron has no seconds field — defaults to starting at second 0.
cron.formatEan13: Minutes: 0-59. * means every minute, */5 means every 5 minutes, 0,30 means minutes 0 and 30, 10-20 means minutes 10 through 20.
cron.formatUpc: Hours: 0-23. 9-17 means 9 AM to 5 PM, */2 means every 2 hours. Note it's 24-hour format — 3 PM is 15, not 3.
cron.featureOnline: * (Asterisk): "Every" — no restriction on this field, matches all possible values. E.g., * in the minute field means triggered every minute.
cron.featurePreview: / (Slash): "Interval" — starting from the initial value, triggers every N units. E.g., */10 in the minute field means every 10 minutes (0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50).
cron.featureExport: - (Hyphen): "Range" — a continuous interval from A to B. E.g., 9-17 in the hour field means 9 AM to 5 PM.
cron.featureSecurity: , (Comma): "List" — enumerates multiple discrete values. E.g., MON,WED,FRI means Monday, Wednesday, Friday.
cron.usageClickUpload: Enter Expression: Type a Cron expression in the input box — e.g., 0 30 9 * * MON.
cron.usageFormats: Select Format: 5-field (standard Cron) or 6-field (seconds extension). The tool auto-detects the field count.
cron.usagePreview: Real-time Parsing: After input, the tool parses each field's meaning and displays a description. E.g., "Every day at 9:30, Monday to Friday."
cron.usagePreset: Visual Generation: Select values for minute/hour/day/month/weekday via dropdown menus — the tool auto-generates the corresponding Cron expression.
cron.usageCustom: Preset Templates: Built-in common expressions — every minute (* * * * *), daily at midnight (0 0 * * *), every 30 minutes on workdays (0/30 9-17 ? * MON-FRI), etc.
cron.usageColorValue: Expression Preview: The Cron expression is displayed in real time during generation — can be directly copied to crontab or Spring configuration.
cron.usageToleranceDef: Next 10 Executions: The tool calculates the next 10 execution time points based on the current time — convenient for verifying whether the expression meets expectations.
cron.usageToleranceLarge: Time Validation: If predicted execution times are clearly wrong (e.g., you expect daily but results show monthly), the expression is incorrect — go back and check field meanings.
cron.usageToleranceSmall: Boundary Cases: Non-existent dates like Feb 30 or leap year Feb 29 are automatically skipped — the Cron engine only triggers on actually existing dates.
cron.usageToleranceDefault: Timezone Note: Cron expression execution times are based on the server timezone — this tool uses the browser's local timezone for prediction. If the server is in a different timezone, actual execution times may differ.
cron.usageApply: Every minute: * * * * * — simple but use cautiously; high-frequency tasks may put pressure on the server.
cron.usageRealPreview: Every hour on the hour: 0 * * * * — minute field is 0, other fields are *.
cron.usageDownload: Daily at 3 AM: 0 3 * * * — suitable for maintenance tasks like data backups and log cleanup.
cron.usageColorDetect: Matching Mechanism: The Cron daemon wakes up every minute and checks whether the current time matches any expression in the crontab. If it matches, the corresponding command is executed.
cron.usagePixelReplace: Field Independence: The five fields have an AND relationship — they only trigger when all fields match. When both day and weekday fields are specified, they take an OR relationship (this is specified by the POSIX standard and is often confusing).
cron.usageEdge: Execution Guarantee: Cron doesn't guarantee second-level precision — if system load is high, actual execution may be delayed by several seconds. For tasks requiring precise timing, consider using systemd timers or dedicated schedulers.

file-size.problem1: Hard drive manufacturers label 1TB = 1000GB, but the operating system shows only 931GB — because disk manufacturers use decimal (1KB = 1000B), while the OS uses binary (1KiB = 1024B). This "1000 vs 1024" debate has gone on for decades. This tool supports both standards simultaneously: SI standard (1000-based, for disks/networking) and IEC standard (1024-based, for memory/OS).
file-size.problem2: Enter any value and unit, and the tool instantly converts to all other units — from bytes (B) to YB (yottabytes), covering 17 orders of magnitude. Supports decimal input and scientific notation — e.g., 1.5e9 means 1.5 billion bytes.
file-size.problem3: Display all unit conversions simultaneously without repeated calculations.
file-size.unitByte: Byte (B): The smallest storage unit. 1 English character = 1 Byte.
file-size.unitKb: Kilobyte (KB): Common for small file sizes.
file-size.unitMb: Megabyte (MB): Common for images and music files.
file-size.unitGb: Gigabyte (GB): Common for videos and system images.
file-size.unitTb: Terabyte (TB): Common for hard drive capacity.
file-size.formatTitle: 2. The Difference Between the Two Standards
file-size.formatBin: SI Standard (decimal, 1000-based): 1KB = 1000B, 1MB = 1000KB, 1GB = 1000MB. Hard drive manufacturers, network equipment, and disk formatting use this standard. Unit symbols are KB, MB, GB (without 'i').
file-size.formatOct: IEC Standard (binary, 1024-based): 1KiB = 1024B, 1MiB = 1024KiB, 1GiB = 1024MiB. Operating systems, memory capacity, and software licensing use this standard. Unit symbols are KiB, MiB, GiB (with 'i').
file-size.formatDec: Why the Difference? 1000GB (manufacturer label) = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. 1024GiB (OS display) = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes. The two differ by about 10% — which is why a 1TB hard drive only shows 931GB on a computer.
file-size.formatHex: Practical Impact: You buy hard drives by manufacturer label (SI), but the OS calculates by IEC — the difference isn't "missing space" but different measurement standards. Network bandwidth also uses SI — 100Mbps = 100,000,000 bits/second.
file-size.featureRealtime: Real-time Conversion: All unit results update instantly as you type — no button click needed.
file-size.featureDualStandard: IEC & SI Dual Standard Comparison: Clearly labels each unit's conversion base — IEC standard where 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes (2^20), SI standard where 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes (10^6). The results panel shows both exact byte count and human-readable formatted results, eliminating the confusion of "why does my 500GB drive only show 465GB."
file-size.featureCopy: One-click Copy: Each conversion result has an independent copy button for copying individual unit values. You can also copy the complete conversion table for pasting into documents, spreadsheets, or code comments.
file-size.featureSecurity: Pure Front-end Computation: All conversions are done in the browser — no data is uploaded.
file-size.featureOnline: Full Unit Coverage: From B (bytes) to YB (yottabytes) — 17 units covering all possible file size ranges. Displays both SI and IEC standard results simultaneously.
file-size.featurePreview: Real-time Conversion: All unit results update instantly after entering a value — no need to click a "Convert" button.
file-size.featureExport: One-click Copy: Each unit's conversion result can be copied with one click — convenient for pasting into documents or code.
file-size.usageIec: IEC Standard (1024-based): 1 KB = 1024 B. Used by Windows OS, memory capacity, etc.
file-size.usageSi: SI Standard (1000-based): 1 KB = 1000 B. Used by disk/USB manufacturers, network bandwidth, etc.

file-size.usageColorValue: Bandwidth Conversion: Network bandwidth 100Mbps = 12.5MB/s — converting bits to bytes requires dividing by 8.
file-size.usageToleranceDef: Quick Estimation: 1GB ≈ 1000MB ≈ 1 billion bytes. Use 1000-based for daily estimation, 1024-based for precise calculations.
file-size.usageToleranceLarge: Hard Drive Capacity: A manufacturer-labeled 500GB drive shows about 465GB in the OS — about 7% difference, which is normal.
file-size.usageToleranceSmall: Memory Capacity: 8GB memory = 8 × 1024MB = 8192MB — memory always uses 1024-based calculation.
file-size.usageToleranceDefault: Network Speed: 100Mbps broadband ≠ 100MB/s download speed. Actual max download speed = 100/8 = 12.5MB/s.
file-size.usageApply: Standard Selection: Storage devices (HDD/SSD) use SI standard, memory and OS use IEC standard, network bandwidth uses SI standard.
file-size.usageRealPreview: Precision Note: Large unit conversions may have floating-point precision errors — the tool automatically keeps reasonable decimal places.
file-size.usageDownload: Data Security: Pure front-end computation, no data is uploaded.
file-size.usageColorDetect: Q: Why does my hard drive capacity seem "shrunk"? A: It's not shrunk — manufacturers label 1TB = 10^12 bytes, the OS displays ÷ 2^40 bytes = 1TiB. The actual byte count is the same.
file-size.usagePixelReplace: Q: KB or KiB — which is correct? A: Depends on context. Disks/networking use KB (1000-based), OS/memory uses KiB (1024-based). Strictly speaking KB should mean 1000, but many software tools mix them up.
file-size.usageEdge: Q: How to calculate file transfer time? A: File size (bytes) ÷ transfer speed (bytes/second) = transfer time (seconds). Note the unit consistency — bandwidth is usually in bit/s, file size in Byte.
file-size.notesDiffTitle: 1. Why Does My Hard Drive Show Less Capacity Than Advertised?
file-size.noteDiff: Hard drive manufacturers use SI standard (1000-based), while operating systems use IEC standard (1024-based). For example, a 500GB drive: manufacturer calculates 500×1000³, system displays ÷1024³ ≈ 465 GiB. This is normal, not a quality issue.
file-size.notePrecision: Results are displayed with up to 6 significant digits. Very small or very large values may have minor floating-point precision differences.
